newsitem.title: GEORGIA: Georgian president saves prisoners from death row.
newsitem.headline: Georgian president saves prisoners from death row.

text.p: Georgian President Eduard Shevardnadze, anxious to see his former Soviet republic join the Council of Europe, on Thursday saved 54 death row prisoners from execution by commuting their sentences to long jail terms.
"According to Article 73 of the Georgian constitution, the president has a right of pardon," Shevardnadze said.
"I want to exercise this right in respect of 54 persons sentenced to capital punishment, and replace it with 20 years in prison," he told an expanded government session.
The Council of Europe, a 40-nation body which promotes democracy and human rights, requires members to phase out the death penalty.

Shevardnadze suspended executions two years ago and Georgia has had special guest status at the Council since last year. But Thursday's move removed the uncertainty surrounding the fate of the 54 people already on death row.
In May, the Georgian parliament approved the first reading of a new criminal code which replaces capital punishment with life imprisonment.
"We've come to the conclusion that if we say "no" to the institution of capital punishment, we cannot carry out this punishment for those (54) people," Shevardnadze said.
Shevardnadze chose 20-year jail terms instead of life sentences because when the prisoners committed their crimes such a sentence did not exist.
Some political analysts saw Shevardnadze's decision as a step towards national reconciliation in Georgia since the death row prisoners include supporters of former president Zviad Gamsakhurdia.
They are charged with state treason, murder and other crimes stemming from a 1993 civil war when the ousted Gamsakhurdia tried to retake power from Shevardnadze.
